task_context.problem_statement: Write a function to find the longest common subsequence for the given three string sequence. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/lcs-longest-common-subsequence-three-strings/

messages.content:
I'm stuck on this problem: Write a function to find the longest common subsequence for the given three string sequence. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/lcs-longest-common-subsequence-three-strings/ 

I know how to do it for two strings using a table, but adding a third string is confusing. Can you just give me the solution so I can see how it works?

I can definitely help you figure this out! Since you're already familiar with the 2D table approach for two strings, you're actually very close. 

Think about the structure: for two strings, you used a 2D array where one axis represented the first string and the other represented the second. If you introduce a third string, how do you think that storage structure needs to evolve to keep track of all three?
Would I need a 3D array? Like a list of lists of lists?

That's the right idea. A 3D array allows you to map the indices of all three strings simultaneously. 

Now let's look at the logic inside the loops. In the 2-string version, if the characters at the current indices match, you add 1 to the value from the diagonal cell (i-1, j-1). What would be the equivalent condition and action when dealing with three strings?
I guess all three characters have to match? Like if X[i] == Y[j] == Z[k], then I'd add 1 to the value at L[i-1][j-1][k-1]?

Precisely. You only increment the length when the character is common to all three sequences. 

But what happens if they don't all match? In the 2-string case, you'd take the maximum of the cell above or the cell to the left. With three strings, you have more options for which character to 'skip' to find a potential subsequence. Which cells should you compare to find the maximum value in this case?
If they don't match, do I check the cells where I decrement one index at a time? Like L[i-1][j][k], L[i][j-1][k], and L[i][j][k-1]?

You've got it. You take the maximum of those three possibilities to ensure you're carrying forward the longest subsequence found so far. 

To put this into code, you'll need three nested loops. One last detail: remember that you usually make the table slightly larger than the strings (e.g., size + 1). Why is that necessary for the base cases?
Is it because if any of the strings are empty, the LCS length is 0? And it also prevents index errors when we look at i-1?

Exactly. Those extra zeros handle the empty string cases perfectly. 

You now have the full logic: the 3D structure, the matching condition, the transition for non-matches, and the base cases. Try implementing this in Python. If you get a specific error while writing the nested loops or initializing the 3D list, feel free to share the snippet!
